# A release is a promise {#sec-shipping}

A release is more than a built executable. It is an identified package that runs on a user's
machine, includes its notices, and can be supported after it ships.

## Install before you package {#sec-deploy}

Install into a clean prefix, then let Qt's deployment script collect the QML modules, plugins,
and libraries it needs. Test that result away from the development machine.

Deployment is platform-specific. A macOS application uses a bundle, Windows needs DLLs beside
the executable, and Linux packages need their runtime dependencies arranged for the target
system. CPack wraps the installed files in a platform-specific package. Test the package on a
clean machine: a development machine may hide missing plugins or libraries.

The template currently packages a disk image on macOS, a ZIP archive on Windows, and a TGZ
archive on Linux. Other package formats may suit your audience better. On Windows, Qt's deploy
step knows its own DLLs; the install rules also copy other runtime DLLs required by the app.
Qt plugins load at runtime, so a missing platform plugin may only become visible on a clean
machine.

::: {.snippet source="src/app/CMakeLists.txt"}

```cmake
install(TARGETS app
    RUNTIME DESTINATION "${CMAKE_INSTALL_BINDIR}"\n)
```

:::

After installing the executable, the template generates and installs Qt's deployment script:

::: {.snippet source="src/app/CMakeLists.txt"}

```cmake
qt_generate_deploy_qml_app_script(
install(SCRIPT "${_deploy_script}")
```

:::

The script runs during installation, after the app is in place. It collects Qt's required
libraries, plugins, and QML imports for the supported deployment platform.

## Versions describe user impact {#sec-versions-and-backports}

For an application, a version tells users what upgrade they are taking. Use the three SemVer
numbers as a clear expectation:

| Release | User expectation |
|---|---|
| Patch, `1.2.1` | fixes a problem without changing normal use |
| Minor, `1.3.0` | adds compatible capability |
| Major, `2.0.0` | makes an incompatible change to a supported contract |

A tag such as `v1.2.1` identifies the exact source of a release. Define what users may rely
on, for example a document format or CLI command. Internal refactoring is not a major release.
Before `1.0.0`, SemVer treats the public API as unstable, so communicate compatibility
expectations directly to users.

## Maintenance branches keep fixes traceable {#sec-backports}

Support an older release only when users need it. Fix and test the issue on the main line,
then copy the small, tested fix to the maintenance branch.

```sh
git switch release/1.2
git cherry-pick -x <fix-commit>
```

The `-x` trailer records the source commit when the pick applies without conflicts. After
resolving a conflict, check the message and add the reference if needed. That trace matters
when a future fix needs the same branch. Release the backport with its own patch tag.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[Release 1.2.0] --> B[Later work on main] --> C[Fix on main]
    A --> D[Maintenance branch 1.2] --> E[Backport and release 1.2.1]
    C -. cherry-pick .-> E
```

## CI makes the package repeatable {#sec-ci}

A release workflow should build, test, deploy, package, and archive the result on every
supported platform. Symbol files make crash reports useful, so a production release process
must preserve matching debug symbols before removing debug information from distributed
binaries. The template archives application symbols separately from each release package: a
`.dSYM` on macOS, a linker `.pdb` with MSVC on Windows, and a `.debug` file on Linux.
The symbol artifact includes the commit, version, platform, and architecture. Keep it with the
matching package; rebuilding the same commit does not guarantee matching binary identities.

Packaging removes debug information from the staged macOS and Linux application while keeping
function symbols for runtime traces. The build-tree executable stays unchanged. Windows keeps
debug information in its separate PDB. The archive covers the application and its linked static
code, not the deployed Qt libraries or other shared dependencies. Preserve matching dependency
symbols separately when you need to diagnose those libraries.

Use the archive for offline analysis: match a macOS crash report's binary UUID to the dSYM
with `dwarfdump --uuid`, load the matching executable and `.debug` file into GDB on Linux,
or load the matching executable and PDB into Visual Studio or WinDbg on Windows. The commit
metadata helps locate a build; the debugger's binary identity check establishes the symbol
match. Keep the exact distributed executable as well as its symbols.

Application logs can capture handled errors and stack traces while the process still runs.
The template does not collect operating-system crash reports or minidumps automatically, and
it has no crash-report upload service. External symbols support investigation once you obtain
a crash report or dump; they do not add crash collection.

The template's release workflow is started manually. It builds and tests on the configured
platforms, packages the app, and uploads workflow artifacts for inspection. Download and test
those artifacts before you publish a release; creating a workflow artifact does not itself
publish a GitHub release.

## Licenses travel with the product {#sec-licenses}

Ship notices and required license texts for Qt, libraries, fonts, and other assets. REUSE
keeps the source inventory checkable. Licensing needs project-specific review before release.

Qt and each third-party library, font, and icon may carry different terms. Keep the applicable
notices and license texts with the distributed app, not only in the source repository. The
About dialog provides a way to find the installed notices. `REUSE.toml` records license
information for repository files, and the REUSE check helps find files without coverage.
